γὰρ, οὐχ ὑπέρ γε μᾶλλον ἑαυτοῦ, πολλοῦ γε καὶ δεῖ, ἀλλ' ὑπὲρ πάσης τῆς ὑπ'
οὐρανόν. Καὶ μαρτυρήσει γράφων ὁ πάνσοφος Παῦλος περὶ τοῦ Θεοῦ καὶ Πατρὸς,
ὅτι "6Τοῦ ἰδίου Υἱοῦ οὐκ ἐφεί- σατο, ἀλλ' ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν πάντων παρέδωκεν αὐτὸν, ἵνα
καὶ σὺν αὐτῷ τὰ πάντα ἡμῖν χαρίσηται."6 Καὶ αὐτὸς δέ πού φησι διὰ τῆς τοῦ
Ψάλλοντος λύρας πρὸς τὸν ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς Πατέρα καὶ Θεόν· "6Θυσίαν καὶ
προσφορὰν οὐκ ἠθέλησας, σῶμα δὲ κατηρτίσω μοι. Ὁλοκαυτώματα καὶ περὶ
ἁμαρτίας οὐκ εὐδόκησας, τότε εἶπον· Ἰδοὺ ἥκω. Ἐν κεφαλίδι βιβλίου γέγρα-πται
περὶ ἐμοῦ, τοῦ ποιῆσαι, ὁ Θεὸς, τὸ θέλημά σου ἠβουλήθην."6 Ἀνονήτου γὰρ οὔσης
τοῖς ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς εἰς τὸ ἀφελεῖν ἁμαρτίας τῆς κατὰ νόμον λατρείας, ἐπείπερ ἦσαν
ἀβούλητοι τῷ Θεῷ βουθυσίαι τε καὶ προβάτων σφαγαὶ, προσκεκόμικεν ἑαυτὸν εἰς
ὀσμὴν εὐωδίας ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν ὁ ἀμνὸς ὁ ἀληθινὸς, ὁ αἴρων τὴν ἁμαρτίαν τοῦ κόσμου·
εἶτα τὸν τῆς σαρκὸς ὑπομείνας 70.1176 θάνατον, ὅλην ἠλευθέρωσε τὴν ὑπ'
οὐρανὸν, καὶ θανάτου, καὶ ἁμαρτίας. Εἶς γὰρ ὁ πάντων ἀνταξιώ- τερος πέπονθεν
ὑπὲρ πάντων, ἵνα πάντων κρατῇ τε καὶ βασιλεύῃ. Καὶ πιστώσεται πάλιν ὁ Παῦλος
γρά- φων· "6∆ιὰ τοῦτο Χριστὸς ἀπέθανε καὶ ἔζησεν, ἵνα καὶ νεκρῶν καὶ ζώντων
κυριεύσῃ."6 Καὶ πάλιν· "6Εἶς ὑπὲρ πάντων ἀπέθανεν, ἵνα οἱ ζῶντες μηκέτι ἑαυ- τοῖς
ζῶσιν, ἀλλὰ τῷ ὑπὲρ αὐτῶν ἀποθανόντι καὶ ἐγερθέντι."6 Ὀρθῶς οὖν ὁ προφήτης
φησὶν, ὅτι "6Οὗτος ὁ ἐν πληγῇ ὢν ὁ εἰδὼς φέρειν μαλακίας, ὁ ἀπεστραμμένον ἔχων
τὸ πρόσωπον, ὁ ἀτιμασθεὶς, καὶ μὴ λογισθεὶς, τὰς ἡμῶν ἁμαρτίας φέρει, καὶ περὶ
ἡμῶν ὀδυνᾶται, καὶ ἡμεῖς ἐλογισάμεθα αὐτὸν εἶναι ἐν πόνῳ, καὶ ἐν πληγῇ, καὶ ἐν
κακώσει."6 Ἄθρει δή μοι πάλιν, μεθ' ὅσης εὐτεχνίας ὁ προφητικὸς ἐν τούτοις
πρόεισι λόγος. Ὑποπλάττεται γὰρ πρόσωπον τῶν μὴ εἰδότων τὸ Χριστοῦ μυστήριον,
οἰηθέντων δὲ ὅτι γέγονεν ἐν τῷ παθεῖν, ὡς ἰδίων ἁμαρτημάτων ἀποστήσων.
Ἐλογισάμεθα γὰρ αὐτὸν εἶναι ἐν πόνῳ, καὶ ἐν πληγῇ, καὶ ἐν κακώσει, φησὶ,
τουτέστιν, ἐνομί- σαμεν θεήλατον ἐπ' αὐτῷ συμβῆναι τὸ πάθος, ὡς διά τινας
ἁμαρτίας, ταύτης τε ἕνεκα τῆς ἁμαρτίας ἐν πόνῳ, καὶ ἐν πληγῇ, καὶ ἐν κακώσει
γενέσθαι. Τὸ δὲ οὐχ οὕτως ἔχει ποθὲν, ἀλλ' ἐτραυματίσθη μᾶλλον διὰ τὰς ἁμαρτίας 433 ἡμῶν, καὶ μεμαλάκισται διὰ τὰς ἀνομίας ἡμῶν. Εἶτα καὶ ἑτέρους ἀποδίδωσι λόγους,
δι' ὧν ἔστιν ἰδεῖν, ὅτι τῆς ἡμετέρας ἕνεκα σωτηρίας, καὶ ζωῆς, γέγονεν ἐν τῷ παθεῖν
ὁ μὴ εἰδὼς ἁμαρ- τίαν. Πάλαι μὲν γὰρ διειστήκειμεν εἰς ἔχθραν τῷ Θεῷ, τοῖς ἱεροῖς
αὐτοῦ μαχόμενοι νόμοις, καὶ τὸν τῆς εὐπειθείας οὐκ ἔχοντες ζυγὸν, καὶ τὸ
δουλεύειν αὐτῷ παραιτούμενοι. Ἀλλ' ἦν ἀναγκαῖο
pass_a_gloss: [...] so that, as Paul says, he might sanctify the people through his own blood; for he suffered, not rather for himself, far from it, but for the whole [world] under heaven. And the all-wise Paul will bear witness, writing about the God and Father that: His own Son he did not spare, but for us all he handed him over, so that also with him he may grant all things to us. And he himself also says somewhere through the lyre of the one who sings psalms to the Father and God in the heavens: Sacrifice and offering you did not wish, but a body you prepared for me. Whole burnt offerings and [offerings] for sin you did not take pleasure in; then I said: Behold, I come. In the head of a book it is written about me; to do, O God, your will I wished. For the worship according to the law being useless for those on the earth for taking away sin, since ox-sacrifices and slaughters of sheep were unwilled by God, the true lamb, the one taking away the sin of the world, brought himself for us into a smell of fragrance; then, having endured the death of the flesh, he freed the whole [world] under heaven both from death and from sin. For one worth more than all suffered for all, so that he might rule and reign over all. And Paul will confirm again, writing: Because of this Christ died and lived, so that he might be lord of both dead and living. And again: One died for all, so that those living may no longer live for themselves, but for the one who died for them and was raised. Rightly then the prophet says that, This one being in blow, the one who knows to bear sicknesses, the one having the face turned away, the one dishonoured and not reckoned, bears our sins, and is pained for us, and we reckoned him to be in toil, and in blow, and in affliction. Look then again with me with how much skill the prophetic word goes forward in these. For it puts on a person of those not knowing the mystery of Christ, but having thought that he came to be in suffering as going to pay for his own sins. For we reckoned him to be in toil and in blow and in affliction, he says, that is, we thought the suffering happened upon him driven by God, as because of some sins, and that for the sake of this sin he came to be in toil, and in blow, and in affliction. But it is not so at all, but rather he was wounded because of our sins, and made weak because of our lawlessnesses. Then he gives also other words through which it is possible to see that for the sake of our salvation and life the one who did not know sin came to be in suffering. For of old we stood apart in enmity toward God, fighting his holy laws, and not having the yoke of obedience, and refusing to serve him. But it was necessa[ry] [the section breaks off].
pass_b_english: … so that, as Paul says, he might sanctify the people through his own blood (Hebrews 13:12). For he suffered not for himself (far from it) but for the whole world under heaven.

The all-wise Paul will bear witness, writing of God the Father: “He did not spare his own Son, but gave him up for us all, so that with him he might also give us all things” (Romans 8:32). And the Son himself says somewhere, through the lyre of the Psalmist, to his Father and God in heaven: “Sacrifice and offering you did not want, but a body you prepared for me. In whole burnt offerings and sin offerings you took no pleasure. Then I said, ‘Here I am, I have come; in the scroll of the book it is written of me.’ To do your will, O God, I have desired” (Psalm 40:6–8; compare Hebrews 10:5–7).

The worship under the Law was of no use to those on earth for taking away sin, since the sacrifices of oxen and the slaughter of sheep were not what God wanted. So the true Lamb, “who takes away the sin of the world” (John 1:29), offered himself for us “as a fragrant aroma” (Ephesians 5:2). Then, having endured death in the flesh, he set the whole world under heaven free from both death and sin. For One who outweighs all in worth suffered for all, so that he might rule and reign over all.

Paul will confirm this again when he writes: “For this reason Christ died and lived, so that he might be Lord of both the dead and the living” (Romans 14:9). And again: “One died for all, so that those who live might no longer live for themselves, but for him who died and was raised for them” (2 Corinthians 5:14–15).

Rightly, then, the prophet says: “This man, who was under the blow, who knew how to bear sickness, whose face was turned away, who was dishonored and not esteemed, bears our sins and suffers pain for us; and we reckoned him to be in toil, under a blow, and in affliction” (Isaiah 53:3–4).

Look again, I ask you, with what skill the prophetic word moves forward here. It takes on the part of those who did not know the mystery of Christ, and who thought that he came to suffer as one paying for his own sins. “For we reckoned him to be in toil, under a blow, and in affliction,” he says; that is, we supposed that the suffering had come upon him from God, as if for some sins, and that he was in toil, under a blow, and in affliction because of that sin.

But it is not so at all; rather, “he was wounded because of our sins, and made weak because of our lawless deeds” (Isaiah 53:5). Then he gives further reasons, through which one can see that he “who knew no sin” (2 Corinthians 5:21) came to suffer for the sake of our salvation and life.
For long ago we stood apart from God in enmity, fighting against his holy laws, not bearing the yoke of obedience, and refusing to serve him. But it was necessary …

choices.english: as one paying for his own sins
choices.why: The printed participle is odd (perhaps for ἀποτίσων); the next sentence makes the sense plain.
rejected: as one who would remove his own sins

choices.why: Isaiah 53:3 Septuagint; not 'whose face is set towards the afflicted'.
rejected: has his face set towards the afflicted

choices.english: One who outweighs all in worth
choices.why: The one Christ is of more worth than all for whom he died.

choices.english: had come upon him from God
choices.why: The onlookers supposed the suffering was a punishment sent by God.

choices.english: he was wounded because of our sins
choices.why: Cyril has the two nouns the other way round from the Septuagint of Isaiah 53:5; the English follows Cyril, and the sentence stands once.
